why_how.text: The vision test outcome shapes the license: passing only with lenses adds a lens requirement, and failing brings a specialist's vision statement.
Interpreters may help on written tests, but commercial license tests are the exception.

scenario.text: Luis speaks limited English and is taking the operator's license knowledge test.

reasoning.text: Foreign language interpreters may help on every written test except commercial license knowledge tests.

result.text: Luis may use an interpreter for his operator's knowledge test.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking interpreters are banned from every licensing test.

correction.text: Interpreters may assist on every written knowledge test except commercial license tests, and they may relay instructions in non-commercial skills tests.

prompt.text: You pass the vision test only while wearing your contacts. What does your license require?

answer.text: That you wear glasses or contacts while driving.

rationale.text: Needing lenses to pass the vision test puts a lens requirement on the license.

lines.text: Health questions and a vision test.

narration.text: This lesson covers the first checks at the counter: a few health questions, the vision test, and the written knowledge test. These checks decide whether your application moves forward and whether your license carries any conditions. We will look at what happens when there is doubt about your fitness to drive, what the vision results mean for you, when to arrive for a knowledge test, and how interpreters may help. Pay attention to the exceptions, especially the one for commercial licenses, because that is where practice questions like to set traps.

lines.text: Staff ask a few health questions.
A reexamination may need medical information.

narration.text: Staff ask a few general health questions when you apply. If there is doubt about your physical fitness to drive, your application can be held pending a reexamination with more medical information. That does not mean you are refused. It means the state wants more information before deciding. Think of it as a hold on the paperwork rather than a final answer. When a practice question describes a doubt about fitness, the expected result is a held application and a reexamination, not an automatic denial and not an automatic approval.

lines.text: Pass with lenses: wear them to drive.
Limits like daylight only may follow.

narration.text: The vision test has two outcomes worth knowing. If you need glasses or contacts to pass, your license will require you to wear them while driving. If you fail the vision test, an eye-care specialist must complete a vision statement, and limits such as daylight driving only may follow. So passing with lenses brings a lens requirement, while failing brings a specialist report and possible limits. Keep those two paths apart. A daylight-only limit is tied to the failing path, and the lens requirement is tied to passing with correction.

For a knowledge test toward an original operator's, chauffeur's or commercial license, arrive at least one hour before the office closes. Knowledge tests come in many languages, and foreign language interpreters may help on every written test except commercial license knowledge tests. In the skills test, hard-of-hearing or non-fluent applicants may use an interpreter, who must show photo ID and only relay the examiner's instructions, but not in commercial license written or skills tests. The commercial exception runs through every interpreter rule, so remember it as the one place interpreters cannot help.

Here is the trap. Some learners assume interpreters are not allowed on licensing tests at all. That is not true. Interpreters may assist on every written knowledge test except commercial license tests, so a non-fluent car applicant can use one for the knowledge test. In a non-commercial skills test, an interpreter may also help, but only by relaying the examiner's instructions after showing photo ID. The opposite trap also appears, where an option claims interpreters can help with a commercial test. They cannot. Ask whether the test is commercial before deciding.

Here is a quick check: you pass the vision test, but only while wearing your contacts. What does your license require from now on? Recall the two vision paths. Passing only with glasses or contacts means the license will require you to wear them while driving. So the answer is that you must wear your contacts or glasses whenever you drive. You do not need a specialist's statement, because that belongs to the failing path. And there is no daylight-only limit here either, because that kind of limit may follow a failed vision test instead.

To wrap up the counter checks, remember these points. Health questions come first, and doubt about your fitness can hold the application for a reexamination with more medical information. If you need glasses or contacts to pass the vision test, the license requires them; if you fail, an eye-care specialist completes a statement and limits may follow. Arrive at least an hour before closing for an original license knowledge test. Tests come in many languages, and interpreters may help on every written test and non-commercial skills test, but never on commercial tests.

why_how.text: A TIP is a practice permit: it lasts one hundred eighty days and lets you practice with a licensed adult before the skills test.
The thirty days of practice are required, while the adult driver education course is only encouraged.

scenario.text: Dev, never licensed, received his TIP and wants to book the skills test two weeks later.

reasoning.text: You must practice on a TIP for at least thirty days before the driving skills test.

result.text: Dev must wait until he has practiced at least thirty days.

claim.text: Myth: an adult driver education course is required before the skills test.

correction.text: The thirty-day TIP practice minimum is required, and the adult driver education course is only encouraged, not required.

prompt.text: Which is required on a TIP: thirty days of practice or an adult driver education course?

answer.text: Thirty days of practice; the course is only encouraged.

rationale.text: The practice minimum is a firm requirement, while the course is encouraged but not required.

lines.text: How long it lasts and what it takes.

narration.text: This lesson explains the temporary instruction permit, or TIP. It is the permit that lets a new driver practice legally before the driving skills test. We will cover who receives one, how long it lasts, the steps to get it, the practice period you must complete, and how you can drive while waiting for your mailed license after the test. Several numbers appear here: one hundred eighty days, thirty days and four years. Each belongs to a different rule, so we will tie each number to the right idea as we go. Let us begin with the basics.

lines.text: Valid for one hundred eighty days.
For new, foreign, or long-expired drivers.

narration.text: A temporary instruction permit is valid for one hundred eighty days and lets you practice with a licensed adult before the driving skills test. TIPs go to people never licensed, to foreign license holders seeking a Michigan license, and to people whose license expired at least four years ago. So a driver whose license lapsed last year does not fall into the TIP group, while one whose license lapsed five years ago does. The permit is about practice. It is not a license to drive alone, so the licensed adult is always part of the picture.

lines.text: Pass vision, health, knowledge and sign tests.
Pay the fee and take a photo.

narration.text: To get a TIP you bring the four proofs, pass the vision test and health standards plus the written knowledge and road sign tests, pay the fee and have your photo taken. That is a long list, but it follows a sensible order: prove who you are, show you can see and know the rules, then pay and get photographed. The driving skills test is not on this list, because it comes later, after practice. So if a question says you need to pass the skills test to receive your TIP, that option has the order backwards. Keep the order clear.

lines.text: Print a temporary permit from MiLogin.

narration.text: You must practice on a TIP for at least thirty days before the driving skills test, and an adult driver education course is encouraged. After the department receives your skills test results, your license is mailed, and a temporary operator's permit printed from your MiLogin account lets you drive until it arrives. So there are two different temporary papers in this story. The TIP is for supervised practice before the test. The printed temporary operator's permit is for the gap after you pass, while your new license is in the mail.

lines.text: Thirty days of practice is required.

narration.text: Here is the trap. The thirty-day TIP practice minimum is a firm requirement on the TIP page, and the adult driver education course is only encouraged, not required. A practice question may list the course as a must, or may say thirty days is only a suggestion. Both are wrong. A second number trap is the length of the permit. The TIP is valid for one hundred eighty days, which is much longer than the thirty-day practice minimum. Keep the two numbers apart: one hundred eighty days is how long the permit lasts, thirty days is how long you must practice.

Here is a quick check: on a TIP, which of these is required before the driving skills test, thirty days of practice or an adult driver education course? Think about how each one was described. The thirty days of practice are a firm minimum. The adult driver education course is encouraged, which means it is a good idea but not a must. So the answer is the thirty days of practice. If you chose the course, remember the difference between required and encouraged. That small word difference is exactly what practice questions are built to test.

lines.text: One hundred eighty days of validity.
Temporary permit from MiLogin after passing.

narration.text: To wrap up, a TIP is valid for one hundred eighty days and lets you practice with a licensed adult. It goes to people never licensed, foreign license holders and people whose license expired at least four years ago. To get one, bring the four proofs, pass the vision, health, knowledge and road sign tests, pay the fee and take a photo. Practice at least thirty days before the skills test; an adult driver education course is encouraged but not required. After your results reach the department, a temporary permit printed from MiLogin covers you until the license arrives.

why_how.text: A motorcycle TIP lets a new rider practice on public roads under constant supervision, but it never replaces the endorsement.
The permit is limited: one hundred eighty days each and no more than two in a ten-year period.

scenario.text: Ravi, sixteen, holds a valid Michigan driver's license and has passed the vision and motorcycle knowledge tests.

reasoning.text: A motorcycle TIP requires age sixteen, a valid Michigan driver's license, passing the vision and motorcycle knowledge tests, and the fee.

result.text: Ravi can get a motorcycle TIP once he pays the fee, and his supervisor must be a licensed motorcyclist at least eighteen.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the motorcycle supervisor only needs to be sixteen, like the rider.

correction.text: A motorcycle TIP holder must be at least sixteen, while the licensed motorcyclist supervising that rider must be at least eighteen.

prompt.text: A motorcycle TIP rider wants to carry a friend on an afternoon ride with a supervisor following. Is that allowed?

answer.text: No. A motorcycle TIP rider may not carry passengers.

rationale.text: Motorcycle TIP riders stay under constant visual supervision and may not ride at night or carry passengers.

narration.text: This lesson covers the motorcycle temporary instruction permit, the practice permit for new motorcycle riders. It works a little like the car TIP, but it has its own requirements and some extra limits that are very specific. We will go through what the permit allows, how long it lasts and how many a rider can receive, who qualifies, and the supervision rules that apply on every ride. Two different ages show up in this topic, one for the rider and one for the supervisor, and they are easy to confuse, so we will set them side by side.

lines.text: Constant supervision by an experienced rider.

narration.text: The motorcycle TIP lets a new rider practice on public roads under the constant supervision of an experienced motorcyclist, and it never replaces the endorsement. A motorcycle TIP lasts one hundred eighty days, and no rider receives more than two of them in a ten-year period. So the permit is a bridge to the endorsement rather than a way around it. A rider cannot keep renewing permits forever to avoid earning the endorsement, because the two-permit limit stops that. The goal is to practice and then earn the CY endorsement.

lines.text: Age sixteen and a valid Michigan license.
Pass vision and motorcycle knowledge tests.
Supervisor licensed and at least eighteen.

narration.text: A motorcycle TIP requires age sixteen, a valid Michigan driver's license, passing the vision and motorcycle knowledge tests, and the fee. On the road, a motorcycle TIP rider must stay in constant visual supervision of a licensed motorcycle operator aged at least eighteen, and may not ride at night or carry passengers. Those limits apply on every ride. Constant visual supervision means the supervising rider keeps the learner in sight. So a ride at night is out, a passenger is out, and riding without the supervisor in view is out too.

Here is the trap. A motorcycle TIP holder must be at least sixteen, while the licensed motorcyclist supervising that rider must be at least eighteen. Questions may make both ages sixteen, or swap them. Another trap treats the permit as a long-term substitute. A motorcycle TIP lasts one hundred eighty days and a rider gets at most two in a ten-year period, so it bridges to the endorsement rather than replacing it. Watch for options that say the permit can be renewed without limit or that it replaces the endorsement. Both are wrong.

Here is a quick check: a rider with a motorcycle TIP wants to carry a friend on an afternoon ride, with the licensed supervisor following close behind. Is that allowed? Recall the limits on every motorcycle TIP ride. The rider must stay in constant visual supervision of a licensed operator at least eighteen, may not ride at night, and may not carry passengers. Daylight and a supervisor do not change the passenger rule. So the answer is no. The friend cannot ride along until the rider has earned the endorsement and the permit limits no longer apply.

lines.text: No night, no passengers, always watched.

narration.text: To finish, here is the motorcycle permit in a few lines. It lets a new rider practice on public roads under constant supervision and never replaces the endorsement. Each permit lasts one hundred eighty days, and no rider gets more than two in ten years. You need age sixteen, a valid Michigan driver's license, the vision and motorcycle knowledge tests, and the fee. The supervisor must be a licensed motorcyclist at least eighteen who keeps you in sight. No night riding and no passengers. Remember the hook: rider sixteen, watcher eighteen.

why_how.text: A skills test is required for new and returning drivers in specific situations, so knowing the triggers tells you who must test.
Teens and adults reach the test differently: teens need training and a clean ninety days, adults need a TIP and possibly thirty days of practice.

scenario.text: Kim moves to Michigan with a valid license from France and wants a Michigan license.

reasoning.text: Licenses from Canada, Germany or South Korea avoid the skills test, while a license from any other country requires it.

result.text: Kim must take the driving skills test.

claim.text: Many people think any foreign license lets you skip the skills test.

correction.text: Only licenses from Canada, Germany or South Korea avoid the skills test; a license from any other country requires it.

prompt.text: A sixteen-year-old finished all training but had an at-fault crash forty days before the test date. Can they test?

answer.text: No. Under-eighteen applicants need a clean record for the ninety days before the test.

rationale.text: The ninety-day rule bars convictions, civil infractions, suspensions and at-fault crashes before the skills test and Level two application.

lines.text: What teens and adults need first.

narration.text: This lesson is about the driving skills test, the hands-on test of your driving. We will start with who must take it, because not every applicant does. Then we will look at what teens under eighteen need before testing, and what adults need instead, because the two groups follow different paths. Finally, we will see who gives the test, how interpreters may help, and how the test itself is structured, from closed-course maneuvers to on-road driving. Watch for the country list and the ninety-day rule, which show up often in practice.

lines.text: Never-licensed adults; licenses expired over four years.

narration.text: A driving skills test is required for Level two, for never-licensed applicants eighteen or older, when your last license expired more than four years ago, or for a license from a country other than Canada, Germany or South Korea. So a teen moving up to Level two tests, an adult getting a first license tests, a returning driver whose license lapsed five years ago tests, and most foreign license holders test. A newcomer with a valid license from one of those three countries does not. That list of three countries is the one to memorize.

lines.text: Segment two and six months on Level one.
Fifty hours, ten at night, logged.
Clean ninety days before the test.

narration.text: Under-eighteen skills test applicants need Segment two completed, Level one held at least six months, and a log of at least fifty supervised hours with ten at night, kept in The Supervised Driving Guide or the free RoadReady app. Under-eighteen applicants must also have no convictions, civil infractions, suspensions or at-fault crashes in the ninety days right before the skills test and Level two application. So training alone is not enough. A teen who finished everything but got a civil infraction two months ago has to wait until ninety clean days have passed.

lines.text: Adults must hold a TIP first.
Ask about the fee before booking.

narration.text: Applicants eighteen or older must hold a TIP before the skills test, and a thirty-day practice period may be required. Independent businesses approved by the Secretary of State give skills tests, and since the state does not set their fees, ask about pricing before you book. Hard-of-hearing or non-fluent applicants may use an interpreter who shows photo ID and only relays the examiner's instructions, except in commercial tests. So for adults, the key prerequisite is the TIP. For everyone, the test happens at an approved business that sets its own price.

The skills test starts with off-street, closed-course maneuvers, and only after passing them do you take the on-road test that earns the driving skills receipt. The on-road portion includes urban, expressway, rural highway and residential driving, as described in the Driving Skills Test Study Guide. So the order matters. If you do not pass the closed-course maneuvers, you do not move on to the road. On the road you can expect a mix of settings, from busy city streets to expressways, country highways and quiet neighborhoods, so practice in all of them.

lines.text: Trap: adults need a clean ninety days.
Adults: TIP and maybe thirty days.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Under-eighteen applicants need a clean record for the ninety days before the skills test, while adults instead need a TIP and possibly a thirty-day practice period. Options may swap those rules between the groups. A second trap is the country list. Foreign licenses from Canada, Germany or South Korea avoid the skills test, while a license from any other country requires it. So a driver from France, Mexico or Japan tests, even with a valid license. When you see a foreign license in a question, check the country before you decide.

Here is a quick check: a sixteen-year-old has finished Segment two, held Level one for six months and logged fifty hours with ten at night, but had an at-fault crash forty days before the planned test date. Can they take the skills test? Recall the teen record rule. Under-eighteen applicants must have no convictions, civil infractions, suspensions or at-fault crashes in the ninety days right before the test. Forty days is inside that window. So the answer is no. Once ninety clean days have passed, the teen can take the test.

lines.text: Most foreign licenses test; three countries skip.
Teens: training and a clean ninety days.

narration.text: To close, here is the skills test summary. It is required for Level two, never-licensed adults, licenses expired more than four years, and licenses from countries other than Canada, Germany or South Korea. Teens need Segment two, six months on Level one, fifty logged hours with ten at night and a clean ninety days. Adults need a TIP and possibly a thirty-day practice period. Approved independent businesses give the test and set their own fees. The test starts with closed-course maneuvers, then moves to urban, expressway, rural and residential driving.

why_how.text: A physician's statement lets the state review conditions that may affect safe driving, at application or renewal.
Different look-back windows apply: six months for a loss of consciousness, twelve months for chauffeur and commercial holders.

scenario.text: Grace, a commercial license holder, had a fainting spell eight months ago.

reasoning.text: Chauffeur and commercial license holders must have had no blackouts, fainting spells or seizures in the last twelve months.

result.text: Grace does not meet the twelve-month rule for commercial holders.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking probation is just another part of Graduated Driver Licensing.

correction.text: Probation of at least three years is a program separate from GDL, even though teens in GDL are also on probation.

prompt.text: A commercial driver had a seizure ten months ago. Do they meet the medical rule for their license?

answer.text: No. Chauffeur and commercial holders need twelve months free of seizures, blackouts and fainting.

rationale.text: Ten months is inside the twelve-month window that applies to chauffeur and commercial license holders.

narration.text: This lesson covers two topics that follow a driver beyond the first test. The first is medical review: when the state asks a physician to describe a condition that may affect driving, and what happens if a serious condition comes up at renewal. The second is probation, the monitoring program for drivers licensed for the first time. Both topics include time windows that sound alike, such as six months, twelve months and three years. We will tie each window to the right rule so the numbers stay in their places. Let us begin with medical review.

lines.text: May be requested at application or renewal.
For conditions that may affect driving.

narration.text: A Physician's Statement of Examination may be requested at application or renewal for any physical or mental condition that may affect safe driving. A physician or physician's assistant licensed in Michigan or another state completes the statement, describing conditions and medications, and the Driver Assessment Section reviews it. So the doctor does not have to be licensed in Michigan, and the decision is made by the state's review section rather than by the doctor. The statement simply gives the state the medical information it needs to decide.

lines.text: Chauffeur and commercial: twelve clear months.

narration.text: A physician's statement is also required when the state has reason to believe you had a seizure, blackout, fainting spell or other loss of consciousness within the past six months. Chauffeur and commercial license holders face a stricter rule. They must have had no blackouts, fainting spells or seizures in the last twelve months. So the same kind of event is measured against two different windows depending on the license. For a regular license question, think six months and a statement. For a chauffeur or commercial question, think twelve clear months.

lines.text: Illness restrictions may bring periodic reexams.

narration.text: A serious condition reported at renewal leads to a driver reexamination, so start renewing several weeks early. A restricted license for illness may bring periodic reexams. That advice about starting early is practical: a reexamination takes time, and you do not want your license to expire while the review is under way. Periodic reexams mean the state may check in again later if your license is restricted because of an illness. Neither of these is a penalty. They are part of keeping the license matched to your current health.

lines.text: At least three years of probation.

narration.text: Any special licensing conditions or restrictions are printed on the license, and drivers licensed for the first time are on probation for at least three years. New drivers, GDL teens included, stay on probation for at least three years, a monitoring program kept separate from GDL. So an adult who gets a first license is on probation even though they never went through GDL. And a teen in GDL is on probation as well, but the two programs are different. Probation is about monitoring new drivers, whatever their age. Keep them apart.

lines.text: Six months for a physician's statement.
Twelve months for chauffeur and commercial.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A physician's statement looks back six months for any loss of consciousness, while chauffeur and commercial license holders need twelve months free of blackouts, fainting or seizures. Options may use six months for commercial drivers or twelve months for everyone. A second trap is probation. Probation of at least three years is a program separate from Graduated Driver Licensing, even though teens in GDL are also on probation. If an option says probation ends when GDL ends, or that probation is the same as GDL, it is wrong.

Here is a quick check: a commercial license holder had a seizure ten months ago. Do they meet the medical rule for their license? Use the right window. Chauffeur and commercial license holders must have had no blackouts, fainting spells or seizures in the last twelve months. Ten months ago falls inside that twelve-month window, so the answer is no. If you were thinking of the six-month window, that one decides when a physician's statement is required for any driver. The commercial and chauffeur rule is stricter and looks back a full year.

lines.text: Three years of probation, apart from GDL.

narration.text: To wrap up, a Physician's Statement may be requested at application or renewal for any condition that may affect safe driving, completed by a physician or physician's assistant licensed in any state and reviewed by the Driver Assessment Section. It is required when you may have lost consciousness within six months, and chauffeur and commercial holders need twelve months free of such events. A serious condition at renewal brings a reexamination, so start early. First-time drivers are on probation for at least three years, in a program separate from GDL.

why_how.text: A name change begins with Social Security, so the Secretary of State can match your new name, then you pay for a new license.
Your license address must match where you live and your voter card, and changing it is free.

scenario.text: Ella moved across town last week and wants to update her license and her car's records.

reasoning.text: An online address change is free and updates the license, voter registration and vehicle records linked to the license account.

result.text: Ella changes her address online at no cost, and her linked vehicle records update too.

claim.text: Common mistake: believing name and address changes both start online with the Secretary of State and both cost a fee.

correction.text: A name change starts at the Social Security Administration and costs a fee for the new license, while an address change starts with the Secretary of State and is free.

prompt.text: What is the very first step to change the name on your Michigan license?

answer.text: Change your name with the Social Security Administration.

rationale.text: Social Security comes first, then at least three business days, then an office visit with your license and name-change proof.

narration.text: This lesson covers how to keep your license records current when your life changes. A new name and a new address are handled very differently, and the order of steps matters. We will cover where a name change starts, how long to wait, and what it costs. Then we will see why your address must match, what an online change updates, which records are left out, and what can happen if you never report a move. Many people assume both changes work the same way, and that assumption is exactly what practice questions are built around.

lines.text: Wait at least three business days.
Office visit with proof and a fee.

narration.text: To change your name, change it with the Social Security Administration first, wait at least three business days, then bring your license and name-change proof to an office for a new license and fee. Notice the order. The Secretary of State is the second stop, not the first. If you go to the office before updating Social Security, or the same day, the record will not be ready. And the name change is not free. You pay a fee for the new license that shows your new name, which is different from how address changes work.

lines.text: Address must match your residence and voter card.
Free online, in person or by mail.
Online updates ID, voter; offers linked vehicles.

narration.text: Michigan law requires your license address to match your residence and your voter identification card, and address changes are free online, in person or by mail. Submitting an address change online updates your driver's license or state identification card and voter registration, while giving you the opportunity to update addresses on vehicle records connected to your license account. That makes the online route efficient, because one change reaches several records at once. Still, there is a limit to what it reaches. You get the opportunity to update vehicles connected to your license account online, while unlinked vehicles are updated during a vehicle transaction.

lines.text: Trap: both start with the Secretary of State.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A name change starts at the Social Security Administration and costs a fee for the new license, while an address change starts with the Secretary of State and is free. Options may say both are free, or both start online, or that the address change carries the fee. A related trap is about vehicles. Vehicles not linked to your license account get the new address only during a vehicle transaction, and failing to report a move can bring suspension or revocation. So reporting a move is not optional, and not every vehicle updates by itself.

Here is a quick check: you recently married and want your new last name on your Michigan license. What is the very first step? Recall the order. You change your name with the Social Security Administration first. Then you wait at least three business days, and only then do you bring your license and your name-change proof to a Secretary of State office for a new license and fee. If you answered that you start online with the Secretary of State, that is how an address change works, not a name change. The order is the whole point here.

lines.text: Name: Social Security, wait, office, fee.
Address: free, matches residence and voter card.

narration.text: To close, here is the summary. A name change starts with Social Security, then a wait of at least three business days, then an office visit with your license and proof, and a fee for the new license. Your license address must match your residence and voter card, and address changes are free online, in person or by mail. An online change updates your license and voter registration and lets you update linked vehicle records, while unlinked vehicles update during a vehicle transaction. Failing to report a move can bring suspension or revocation. Name costs, address free.

why_how.text: A license usually lasts four years to your birthday, but an under-twenty-one license ends on the twenty-first birthday.
Remote renewal is allowed when no office visit is required, but every twelve years renewal must be in person for vision screening and a photo.

scenario.text: Paul, age seventy, still drives and asks for a free state ID card.

reasoning.text: Drivers sixty-five or older get a free ID only when they voluntarily give up the license, while legally blind people qualify regardless of age.

result.text: Paul does not qualify for a free ID while he keeps his license.

claim.text: Myth: every driver over sixty-five gets a free state ID card.

correction.text: A free state ID goes to drivers sixty-five or older only when they give up the license voluntarily, while legally blind people qualify regardless of age.

prompt.text: Someone has renewed by mail and online for years. When must they renew in person?

answer.text: Every twelve years, at an office with a vision screening and a new photo.

rationale.text: Remote renewal is allowed when no visit is required, but the twelve-year cycle requires an office visit.

narration.text: This lesson covers the life of your license after you have it: when it expires, how the renewal notice reaches you, who cannot renew, the different ways to renew, and the regular in-person visit. We will finish with state ID cards for people who stop driving, including who gets one for free. Watch for two special cases that practice questions like: the expiration date for drivers under twenty-one, and the condition that decides whether a driver sixty-five or older receives a free ID. Each rule has a clear trigger that we will point out.

A license is usually valid four years and expires on your birthday in the year printed on it, except that under-twenty-one licenses expire on the twenty-first birthday. So an eighteen-year-old does not get four years. Their license runs to the twenty-first birthday, no matter when it was issued. The renewal notice goes to the address on record, which is one more reason to keep your address current. Driving without a valid license is illegal, and renewing after expiration adds a late fee, so do not let the date slip by.

lines.text: Missing Social Security or legal presence proof.

narration.text: A suspended, revoked or denied license cannot be renewed, and renewal can be refused without a valid Social Security number or ineligibility letter and legal presence proof. So renewal is not automatic. If your license is under a suspension, you must deal with that first. And the state still checks your Social Security status and legal presence at renewal. A practice question might describe a driver trying to renew to get around a suspension. That will not work, because a suspended license cannot be renewed until the suspension is resolved.

lines.text: By mail, online, or self-service station.

narration.text: When no office visit is required, you may renew by mail, online at Michigan dot gov slash SOS, or at a self-service station. Every twelve years you must renew in person at an office, where vision is screened and a new photo is taken. So remote renewal is a convenience, not a permanent replacement for the office. The twelve-year visit keeps your photo current and checks your vision. If a question asks whether a driver who always renews online can skip the office forever, the answer is no. The twelve-year visit still applies.

lines.text: Stop driving: return license, get an ID.
Free for sixty-five-plus who give up driving.

narration.text: Someone who stops driving returns the license to an office and applies for a state ID card instead. Free ID cards go to people who are legally blind, drivers sixty-five or older who voluntarily give up their license, and drivers who lose driving privileges for a physical or mental disability. So the free ID is tied to a situation, not just to age. A driver who is seventy and still driving does not get a free ID. A legally blind person qualifies at any age. And someone who loses driving privileges because of a disability qualifies too.

lines.text: Trap: all sixty-five-plus drivers get free IDs.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A free state ID goes to drivers sixty-five or older only when they give up the license voluntarily, while legally blind people qualify regardless of age. So turning sixty-five alone does not earn a free ID. A second trap is the idea of renewing remotely forever. You may renew by mail, online or at a self-service station when allowed, but every twelve years the renewal must happen in person with a vision screening and photo. When a question offers a shortcut around the office visit or a free ID based only on age, check the condition carefully.

lines.text: When is the office visit due?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a driver has renewed by mail and online for years and hopes never to visit an office again. When must they renew in person? Recall the renewal cycle. Remote renewal is allowed when no office visit is required, but every twelve years you must renew in person at an office, where vision is screened and a new photo is taken. So the answer is every twelve years. If you answered never, remember that remote renewal is a convenience between visits, and the twelve-year visit is the part that cannot be skipped.

lines.text: Four years, or the twenty-first birthday.
Free IDs depend on the situation.

narration.text: To finish, here is the renewal summary. A license usually runs four years to your birthday, while an under-twenty-one license ends on the twenty-first birthday. The renewal notice goes to your address on record, and late renewal adds a fee. Suspended, revoked or denied licenses cannot be renewed. Renew by mail, online or at a self-service station when allowed, and in person every twelve years. If you stop driving, return the license and get a state ID; it is free for legally blind people, drivers sixty-five or older who give up driving, and those who lose privileges for a disability.
